author: Church of Smyrna
addressee: The church of God at Philomelium and all congregations of the holy and catholic church everywhere
occasion: The Smyrnaeans answer a request from Philomelium for a fuller account of their recent martyrs, especially bishop Polycarp, whose death closed the persecution. They want the report circulated to other Christians so God is glorified and Polycarp is remembered and imitated.
argument: True martyrdom happens according to God's will and the gospel: the martyr waits to be handed over like Christ, endures torture patiently with Christ present, and seeks the salvation of others rather than himself. The Smyrnaeans therefore praise the tortured Christians and Germanicus, who provoked the beast, but blame Quintus the Phrygian and other volunteers, whose self-offering ended in denial. Polycarp is the model: he withdrew, prayed constantly, accepted betrayal and arrest, fed his captors, refused the proconsul's demands to swear by Caesar, revile Christ, or deny he was a Christian, and accepted burning in fulfilment of his vision. God vindicated him by shaping the flame around him and by his blood quenching the fire, and Christians rightly worship Christ as Son of God, love the martyrs as disciples and imitators, and keep their bones and yearly memorial without worshipping them.

outline.move: The Smyrnaean church introduces the report: Polycarp sealed the persecution by a gospel-like martyrdom worthy of imitation.

Other martyrs endure flaying, beasts, and the devil's devices with Christ present, Germanicus strengthens them and draws the crowd's demand for Polycarp, while Quintus's voluntary surrender and denial shows why volunteers are not praised.

Polycarp withdraws, prays for all churches, foresees burning alive, is betrayed by members of his own household with a captured boy giving him away under torture, receives arresting officers hospitably, prays at length, and is brought by donkey and cart to the city while refusing Herod and Nicetes' urging to say Caesar is Lord and sacrifice.

In the stadium a heavenly voice encourages Polycarp, he confesses he is a Christian and has served Christ eighty-six years, rejects sacrifice, beasts, and fire by contrasting brief fire with eternal punishment, and the crowd with Jews demands he be burned alive.

Polycarp undresses, refuses nailing, is bound, prays to the Almighty Father through Christ to share the martyrs' cup and resurrection, and the fire arches around him like a sail while he appears as baking bread or refined gold with incense-like fragrance until he is stabbed and much blood quenches the fire.

The devil stirs Jews and Nicetes to withhold the body lest Christians worship Polycarp, so the centurion burns it; the writers explain they worship Christ and love martyrs, later gather Polycarp's more precious than gold bones, and celebrate his birthday to remember past martyrs and train future ones.
The writers say they sent a summary through Marcian at the readers' request, ask that it be forwarded, greet all the saints, and close with doxology.

Later dates, greetings, and transmission notes give Polycarp's martyrdom day and offices, plus alternate copyist chains through Irenaeus, Gaius, Socrates or Isocrates in Corinth, and Pionius, with an anecdote about Irenaeus, Polycarp, and Marcion.

cast.name: Polycarp
cast.who: Bishop of the catholic church in Smyrna, an apostolic and prophetic teacher, called 'the teacher of Asia' by the crowd; the central martyr.

cast.name: Germanicus
cast.who: Young Christian whose defiance of beasts encouraged others and provoked the crowd.

cast.name: Quintus
cast.who: Recently arrived Phrygian Christian whose voluntary self-offering ended in sacrificing.

cast.name: Herod
cast.who: Peace-officer who arrested and brought Polycarp into the stadium.

cast.name: Nicetes
cast.who: Herod's father; rode with him and later sought to withhold Polycarp's body.

cast.name: Alce
cast.who: Named as Nicetes's brother in the dispute over the body.

cast.name: Philip the Asiarch
cast.who: Provincial official asked to throw a lion at Polycarp; said the beast-fights were over.

cast.name: Statius Quadratus
cast.who: Proconsul in the closing date formula.

cast.name: Philip of Tralles
cast.who: High priest named in the closing date formula.

cast.name: Irenaeus
cast.who: Disciple of Polycarp; later teacher in Rome and source for copies.

cast.name: Gaius
cast.who: Copier of the account from Irenaeus's writings.

cast.name: Socrates or Isocrates
cast.who: Copyist in Corinth in the manuscript notes; name varies between endings.

cast.name: Pionius
cast.who: Later copyist who says he recovered the aged text after Polycarp appeared to him.

cast.name: Marcian
cast.who: Brother who carried the Smyrnaeans' summary to Philomelium.

cast.name: Evarestus
cast.who: Scribe who wrote the letter with his whole household.

cast.name: Marcion
cast.who: Heretical teacher rebuked by Polycarp in the added Irenaeus anecdote.

voices.speaker: Heavenly voice
voices.how_marked: narrated as a voice from heaven heard by local Christians present, not seen: φωνὴ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐγένετο

voices.speaker: Polycarp
voices.how_marked: direct quoted speech introduced by ἔφη, εἶπεν, or ἀπεκρίνατο

voices.speaker: Roman proconsul
voices.how_marked: direct quoted persuasion and threats introduced as the proconsul questioning or urging: ἀνηρώτα, ἔπειθεν, λέγων

voices.speaker: Herod and Nicetes
voices.how_marked: reported persuasion beside Polycarp in the carriage: ἔπειθον ... λέγοντες

voices.speaker: Crowd: pagan crowd in 3 and 9, pagans and Jews of Smyrna in 12
voices.how_marked: collective shouts and demands quoted directly: ἐπεφώνησεν, εἶπον, ἐπεβόα, ἠρώτων; in 9 the crowd's cry 'Away with the atheists' is quoted before Polycarp repeats it

voices.speaker: Herald
voices.how_marked: threefold proclamation in the stadium sent by the proconsul: κηρῦξαι τρὶς

voices.speaker: Nicetes, instigated by the devil and backed by the Jews
voices.how_marked: the devil puts Nicetes up to petitioning the magistrate not to give up the body; Nicetes is the speaker of the quoted fear μή ... ἄρξωνται σέβεσθαι (φησίν), the Jews back and strengthen the suggestion and watch the pyre

key_terms.sense: faithful suffering unto death that seals and imitates the gospel
one who confesses Christ under trial and dies rather than deny him
organized persecution and pursuit of Christians
worldwide, shared by all true congregations
openly declare oneself a Christian before authority
denying Christ by swearing, sacrificing, or reviling him
Roman governor presiding over the trial in Smyrna
local officer charged with keeping order and making arrests
provincial leader in charge of festivals and beast-shows
God-given reward and victory for enduring martyrdom
yearly celebration of a martyr's death as entry into life
worship owed to Christ alone as Son of God
crowd's insult against Christians for rejecting pagan gods

scripture: The author gives no formal book citations or Psalm numbers; scriptural language appears as unattributed gospel-like phrases and allusions. An English translator should cite these as allusions in modern chapter-and-verse form: Phil 2:4 in 1, the heavenly-goods saying also found in 1 Cor 2:9 and Isaiah in 2, betrayal by kin in 6 as in Matt 10:21 or Matt 10:36, 'Thy will be done' in 7 as in Matt 6:10, and honor to authorities in 10 as in Rom 13:1, rather than reproducing LXX or Vulgate titles or Old Latin Psalm numbering.
uncertain: Exact year and historical setting: the traditional mid-150s date, the late date under Marcus Aurelius, and the offices named in section 21 cannot all be settled from this text alone.
The Greek says 'I have served him eighty-six years'; only the further inference that he was born a Christian and so was 86 years old is open.
Whether the dove reading in section 16 belonged to the earliest text, since it is textually disputed and bracketed in the source.
Historical identity and offices of Quintus, Philip the Asiarch, Herod, Nicetes, Alce, Philip of Tralles, and Statius Quadratus beyond what the narrative states.
Literary status of the long transmission notes and second ending in section 21, including Socrates versus Isocrates and the Pionius vision account.
